 Seniors Filing in February Will See the First Refunds With the $6,000 Senior Deduction in Them. A Retired Couple Over 65 With $80,000 of Income Gets About $1,400 Back They Didn’t Get Last Year, and Here’s the Income Where It Shrinks
 Vilma Rios Thu, November 12, 2026 at 4:07 AM EST 6 min read Quick Read 
 A retired couple over 65 with $80,000 of income gets about $1,400 more back from the new $6,000-per-person senior deduction, which cuts federal tax in the 12% bracket. 
 The deduction shrinks 6% for every dollar of joint income above $150,000 and disappears entirely at $250,000. 
 Couples must file jointly with both Social Security numbers, and the deduction expires after the 2028 tax year unless Congress extends it. 
 The biggest 401k decisions tend to get made once and never revisited: when to roll it over, what to hold inside it, and when to start taking money out. That is exactly what the report: 401k & IRA Tips and Answers was created to address, and it is free today. Read more here . (Sponsor) 
 Picture a married couple who both turned 65 during 2026. They live on pensions, IRA withdrawals and Social Security, and they file the same way every year. When their 2026 return goes in this February, the new senior deduction alone cuts their 2026 federal tax by about $1,440. 
 Studio Romantic / Shutterstock.com The deduction is worth $6,000 for each qualified individual age 65 or older. The worked math below shows where the $1,440 comes from. The worked math below shows where the $1,400 comes from. It also shows the income level where the break starts to shrink and the point where it goes away. 
 A $6,000 Senior Deduction Hiding in Section 151 
 The deduction lives at 26 U.S.C. § 151(d)(5)(C), the code section that once handled personal exemptions. It applies to any taxable year beginning before January 1, 2029, so 2028 is its last year unless Congress extends it. 
 A spouse qualifies by reaching 65 before the tax year ends. Married couples must file a joint return, and each qualifying spouse's Social Security number must appear on the return. The deduction comes on top of the 2026 standard deduction of $32,200 for married couples filing jointly and the separate age-65 add-on.

 Seniors who were already 65 claimed it on their 2025 returns, since the IRS says it took effect beginning in 2025. The February 2027 filing season is the first time it reaches couples who turned 65 in 2026. The IRS treats you as 65 on the day before your 65th birthday, so a January 1, 2027, birthday still counts for 2026. 
 Story Continues How an $80,000 Retired Couple Saves About $1,400 
 Assumptions: married filing jointly, both spouses 65 by December 31, 2026, standard deduction, and $80,000 of adjusted gross income. That AGI includes the taxable share of their Social Security. 
 2026 Return Line 
 Amount 
 Adjusted gross income 
 $80,000 
 Standard deduction 
 $32,200 
 Age-65 add-ons (2 x $1,650) 
 $3,300 
 Taxable income without senior deduction 
 $44,500 
 Senior deduction (2 x $6,000) 
 $12,000 
 Taxable income with it 
 $32,500 
 For 2026, the 12% bracket for joint filers starts at $24,800 and runs to $100,800. All $12,000 of the deduction comes out of that 12% layer, which cuts the couple's federal tax by $1,440. 
 Whether that turns into a refund depends on withholding. If their withholding was set to match what they would have owed without the senior deduction, the $1,440 comes back as a refund. Compared with last year's return, the refund could be closer to $1,900, because turning 65 also adds the $3,300 age-65 add-on and the 2026 inflation adjustments. 
 Where the Senior Deduction Starts Shrinking: $150,000 
 Each spouse's $6,000 falls by 6% of modified adjusted gross income above $75,000 ($150,000 on a joint return). For most retirees, MAGI is simply AGI, since the add-backs cover only foreign income exclusions. 
 Take a couple with $200,000 of MAGI. Each spouse's deduction falls to $3,000, or $6,000 combined. Their taxable income of $158,500 sits in the 22% bracket, so that $6,000 still saves $1,320. The higher bracket nearly offsets the smaller deduction. 
 The deduction goes away entirely at $250,000 of joint MAGI. Inside the phaseout, every $1,000 of extra income wipes out $120 of deduction and adds $26.40 of tax. That drives the real marginal rate in the 22% bracket to about 24.64% (26.88% in the last few thousand dollars before $250,000, where the couple reaches the 24% bracket). If only one spouse is 65 or older, the deduction shrinks by $60 per $1,000. 
 Three Moves Before December 31 That Protect the Break 
 Size Roth conversions and IRA withdrawals. A couple near $150,000 of MAGI can trim a December conversion to stay below the phaseout. Qualified charitable distributions from an IRA after age 70½ keep the gift out of AGI completely. 
 File jointly, with both Social Security numbers. Filing separately gives up the deduction under the statute's married individuals rule. 
 Reset 2027 withholding. If you'd rather have the $1,440 spread across monthly checks, lower pension withholding or estimated payments for 2027. 
 One limit: the deduction is subtracted after AGI is calculated, so it leaves AGI unchanged. That means it doesn't shrink the taxable share of Social Security or the MAGI that Medicare uses. The 2026 Part B surcharge starts above $218,000 of joint income, which places the $80,000 couple far below it. 
 What to Watch Before the 2027 Filing Season 
 The IRS has already published updated 2027 deduction figures for taxpayers 65 and older, as Kiplinger reported. The $6,000 amount itself stays the same each year because it isn't indexed. The larger date is the end of 2028. Unless Congress acts, the 2028 return is the last one with this deduction, which gives couples in their late 60s three filing seasons to plan around it. 
 A couple deciding how much to convert to a Roth around the $150,000 line should run the numbers with a CPA or fiduciary advisor. The window between the last paycheck and the first RMD is often the cheapest tax environment a retiree ever sees, which is the whole subject of our free Roth conversion guide.
